commits.message:
perf(packaging): declare sideEffects and check the claim holds (rich-packaging-1xv.4) (#120)

* perf(packaging): declare sideEffects and check the claim holds (rich-packaging-1xv.4)

`package.json` declared no `sideEffects` field, so bundlers retained every
module they saw rather than pruning what a consumer never reached. Declare
`"sideEffects": false`.

The field is a promise that any module whose exports go unused may be dropped
whole, so the work was confirming the promise before making it. A scan of all
100 files under `src/` found exactly one module-scope mutation, which the
ticket's premise did not expect: `ANSI_COLOR_NAMES` was built as a literal and
then patched by a top-level `for` loop adding a `grayNN` alias for every
`greyNN` name. Module-local, and therefore harmless to a bundler — and still a
module doing work when you import it, with a table that had two shapes over
time. It is now a pure initializer, `withGrayAliases({…})`. Beyond that the
tree was already clean: no module-scope bare calls, no writes escaping a
module, no side-effect-only imports.

A scan run once is a map of `src/` that drifts with the next module, so
`test/seam/import-time-effects.test.ts` walks every `.ts` under `src/` and
fails on a top-level statement that is not a declaration, on the `static {}`
block of a top-level class, and on `import "./x.js"` with no bindings. Its
accept list is the declaration kinds, so an unanticipated grammar form reports
rather than passing. What it cannot judge is an expression's contents, and that
limit is stated in the rule's header rather than left to be discovered.

Measured on a consumer that constructs a `Console` and prints a string, with
the package resolved as a real package and bundled by vite in app mode: 180,498
bytes minified before, 66,876 after — 62.9% smaller, 111.0 KiB saved, and the
same size a deep import into `dist/core/console.js` costs, so the barrel's
premium over deep-importing is now zero. A second program exercising the box
sets, the alias table and markup was built and run both ways and produced
byte-identical output. Full numbers and method on the ticket.

Gates: lint clean, 2423 tests, demos build, 10/10 chromium demo bundles boot.

* docs(seam): disclose the whole of the import-time gate's blind spot

`runAtImport`'s doc said static blocks "are the only place a declaration hides
one", meaning a statement list. Read as "the only place a declaration hides
import-time work" — which is how it reads — it is false, and a reader trusts
the gate to catch things it does not catch.

A class evaluates its decorators, its `extends` clause, its computed member
names and its static field initializers when it is declared, and the gate
accepts all four: `@register class C {}` and `static y = register(C)` pass.
That is the same limit already disclosed for `export const T = defineTheme(…)`
— an expression's contents — not a second undisclosed one, and saying so is
the fix rather than extending the rule. Extending it is not available: `src/`
holds mobx's `@observable` and a `static baseStyle = ""`, both of which
evaluate on import and do nothing, so a rule over those positions would have
to sort a harmless expression from a working one. That judgement is the line
the rule refuses everywhere else, and it would have been red on the widget set
the day it landed.

Fixtures now pin each accepted form, so the blind spot is a checked fact
rather than a claimed one and anyone extending the rule is told what they
changed.

* fix(seam): read the statements a namespace body runs at import

`namespace Foo { install(); }` returned no finding. TypeScript emits a
non-ambient namespace as an IIFE that runs when the module is evaluated, so
that call runs at import exactly as the top-level `install();` the rule exists
to catch — and a scan that stopped at top-level statements was bypassed by
writing the same call one nesting level down.

This is the class-static-block shape again, not the class-expression blind
spot documented alongside it, and that difference is why it is fixed rather
than disclosed: a decorator is an expression and sorting a harmless one from a
working one is a purity judgement, while a bare statement in a namespace body
is a statement. So `runAtImport` recurses — a namespace body is module scope by
another name, and gets the same rule rather than a second rule shaped like it.
Each statement reports at its own line, so the failure names the call and not
the namespace wrapping it.

`namespace A.B { … }` carries a ModuleDeclaration as its body rather than a
block, and closing only the plain form would have left the dotted spelling as
the hole; the walk follows both. Ambient declarations emit no code, so a
`declare` namespace stops the walk, and `sf.isDeclarationFile` stops a whole
`.d.ts` — which the sweep matches, since it asks for every `.ts` under `src/`.

No namespace exists in `src/` today, confirmed by walking the tree with the
parser rather than grepping for a word that appears everywhere, so this closes
the hole at no cost in false positives.

* fix(seam): count the imports that bind nothing but still run

`isEffectOnlyImport` tested `importClause === undefined`, which is the bare
`import "./x.js"` and nothing else. Two more spellings emit as that same bare
import and were read as declarations: `import {} from "./x.js"`, whose clause is
present but empty, and `import { type T } from "./x.js"`, whose single element is
erased and leaves the braces behind.

The predicate is now the definition rather than the shape — binds no name when
the module runs, and survives erasure. The second arm is what keeps `import type
{}` out of it: that clause binds nothing either, but takes the whole statement
with it when it goes, so reporting it would trade a missed effect for a gate that
is red on a file doing nothing. `every` over no elements folds the empty-brace
spelling into the all-type one rather than making it a case of its own.

* docs(seam): say which of source and emit the gate reads

Review read the accept list as a claim that an `enum` is inert, and proposed
narrowing it to `const` enums on the grounds that a plain one emits an IIFE. The
premise is right and the conclusion does not follow, but nothing in the header
said why, and "the accept list is the declaration kinds, and every other kind
reports" invites exactly that reading.

The gate reads the source somebody wrote, not the JavaScript emitted for it. If
desugaring counted, a class's property definitions and every object literal's
allocation would report too, and the rule would distinguish nothing. What it asks
is whether the author wrote a statement that runs at import — which a `static {}`
block and a namespace body are, and which an enum's members are not.

Where the finding lands is the blind spot already disclosed one paragraph down:
`enum E { A = register() }` needs no `const` to be legal and does run on import,
as an initialiser expression exactly like `defineTheme(…)`. It is now named there
rather than left to be rediscovered, with a fixture pinning it as a known hole,
and the reason the narrowing is unavailable recorded beside it — `isolatedModules`
is on, so `const enum` is unsafe across a module boundary, and `ColorDepth` and
`ControlType` are exported non-const enums that rule would fail on day one.

* docs(seam): stop restating the import-time gate's grammar forms

The sentence naming what the gate catches drifted twice inside one PR. It named
`static {}` as the only declaration carrying a statement list while the scan had
handled namespace bodies since `d4f3ff94`, and it described the bindingless
import as one spelling while `08784aa8` made it three. Review caught the first;
the second was already there underneath it.

Both are the same failure, and adding the missing items would only reset its
clock: the paragraph and `test/seam/import-time-effects.ts`'s header were two
enumerations of one grammar, and the header is the one that sits beside the code
it describes. This file says as much about `HOST_ACCESS` a section up and about
the coverage allowlist a section down — a hand-maintained list of what a machine
already computes will be wrong, and will read as authoritative while it is.

The paragraph now states the rule at the altitude it can hold without drifting
and hands the forms to the header.
